fastidious

/fa-STID-ee-uhs/ - the stress falls on STID · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fastidious means extremely exacting and hard to please about details.

Our fastidious neighbor hoses down her recycling before sorting it by color, then by lid.

Example

The theater hired the fastidious Marisa Duval to dress one show and kept her for twenty years, though every costume fitting became a small trial. She sent back three bolts of velvet because the nap ran the wrong way. Hems were steamed, then checked against a card she carried. An actress once changed a button backstage; Duval spotted it from the wings at forty feet.

Fastidious is the exact word for Duval because she is extremely exacting and hard to please about details — the bar is the point, and almost nothing clears it. A meticulous person pours care into their own work; a fastidious one also sits in judgment, finding the flaw in yours. The word carries that faint chill of a bar set impossibly high.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

picky: Picky is fastidious in street clothes — the everyday word for the same impossible-to-please fussiness, aimed mostly at choices: toppings sent back, seats swapped, brands refused. Fastidious dresses the trait for formal use and points it at standards and details rather than menus.

exacting: Exacting describes the demand itself: a standard set high and enforced, usually on other people's work — the exacting editor requires every rule kept. Fastidious describes the temperament behind such demands, hard to please past reason; meet the exacting bar and you are done, while the fastidious eye keeps hunting.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

easygoing: content with however things turn out

slovenly: careless of neatness and detail altogether

Where it sits · how far the pickiness goes

particular → fastidious → obsessive

particular vs. fastidious: A particular eater has likes and states them; a fastidious one sends the plate back over the parsley.

obsessive vs. fastidious: Obsessive goes past fastidious — the checking never ends, long after every box has been ticked.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fastidi: loathing, squeamish disgust (Latin fastidium)

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together: Fastidi- (Latin fastidium, "loathing, squeamish disgust") + -ous (full of) = full of disgust. The original fastidious person was one too easily revolted — Romans may have built fastidium from fastus (overweening pride) and taedium (weariness), pride and boredom curdled together. The modern sense keeps the squeamishness and aims it at details: so hard to please that almost everything offends.

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin fastidium built nothing else in English — fastidious is the root's only descendant. One possible ingredient, taedium ("weariness"), did survive on its own as tedium, but that family link is a linguists' guess, not a certainty.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / faintly critical

Fastidious describes the person almost nothing satisfies — taste sharpened into squeamishness. Keep the family straight: this unit's meticulous praises care spent on one's own work; methodical describes ordered steps; scrupulous adds a moral conscience. Fastidious alone implies that pleasing its owner is nearly impossible — use it when the bar, not the effort, is the story.
